question: What is the defining characteristic of a paroxysmal disorder?

options.B: Gradual and progressive loss of muscle mass
options.C: Sudden and episodic attacks of symptoms
options.D: Constant pain localized to the extremities

explanation: Paroxysmal disorders are marked by sudden, temporary episodes of altered function that happen intermittently. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h1)

question: Why is taking a witness history crucial when assessing a patient with a paroxysmal disorder?

options.A: Medical imaging fails to show any brain structures at all
options.B: Patients always remember every single detail of the seizure
options.C: Patients usually appear completely normal between acute episodes
options.D: Witnesses can prescribe immediate medications during the attack

explanation: Because physical exams often yield normal findings between attacks, accounts from people who witnessed the event are vital. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h1)

question: Which neurotransmitter primarily provides inhibitory action in the central nervous system?
explanation: Gamma-aminobutyric acid, commonly known as GABA, is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter that helps prevent excessive neuronal firing. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h2)

question: What happens when ion channel defects occur in cerebral neurons?

options.A: Blood flow to the brain permanently increases by fifty percent
options.B: Brain cells immediately stop producing all electrical impulses
options.C: Neurons become hyperexcitable and lower the threshold for attacks
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid production drops to near zero levels

explanation: Faulty ion channels disrupt normal cellular resting potentials, making neurons fire too easily and trigger paroxysmal events. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h2)

question: Which seizure type involves both cerebral hemispheres from the very beginning?
explanation: Generalized seizures originate at some point within and rapidly engage bilaterally distributed networks across both brain hemispheres. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h3)

question: A patient experiences a seizure that starts in one specific area of the temporal lobe while remaining conscious. How is this classified?
explanation: When a seizure originates in a localized region of one hemisphere and awareness remains intact, it is classified as a focal aware seizure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h3)

question: Which environmental factor is a very common trigger for breakthrough seizures?
explanation: Lack of adequate rest significantly lowers the seizure threshold and frequently precipitates acute episodes. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h4)

question: Why does severe hyponatremia trigger acute paroxysmal neurological events?

options.A: Abnormal electrolyte levels alter resting membrane potentials in neurons
options.B: Sodium deficiency stops the liver from metabolizing glucose
options.C: Low blood sodium immediately destroys all frontal lobe brain tissue
options.D: Fluid shifts cause permanent blockage of the carotid arteries

explanation: Electrolyte imbalances like low sodium disrupt the chemical gradients required for stable neuronal membrane function. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h4)

question: What is the primary diagnostic test used to record electrical activity of the brain?
explanation: An electroencephalogram (EEG) measures and records the electrical voltage fluctuations generated by neuronal activity within the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h5)

question: Why is magnetic resonance imaging ordered during the evaluation of a new-onset paroxysmal disorder?

options.A: To detect structural brain lesions like tumors or scars
options.B: To measure the exact electrical resistance of scalp skin
options.C: To check serum electrolyte levels in the bloodstream
options.D: To monitor heart rhythm changes during a seizure

explanation: MRI provides detailed images of brain tissue to uncover physical abnormalities that might be causing the abnormal electrical discharges. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of anti-seizure pharmacotherapy?

options.A: Permanent suppression of all normal body movements
options.B: Complete seizure freedom without adverse effects
options.C: Total replacement of lost brain neurotransmitters
options.D: Immediate surgical removal of the cerebral cortex

explanation: Treatment aims to stop seizures entirely while maintaining the patient's quality of life and avoiding drug toxicity. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h6)

question: What happens if a patient stops taking their anti-seizure medication abruptly?

options.A: Blood pressure drops to dangerous levels within minutes
options.B: The underlying brain disease is usually cured permanently
options.C: It can precipitate severe breakthrough seizures or status epilepticus
options.D: Liver enzymes return to normal baseline values overnight

explanation: Sudden withdrawal of stabilizing medications removes neural suppression, frequently triggering dangerous, continuous seizure activity. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h6)

question: How long must continuous seizure activity last to be classified as status epilepticus?
explanation: Status epilepticus is diagnosed when a single seizure lasts past five minutes or when seizures repeat without recovery between them. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h7)

question: What is the correct immediate nursing action when a patient begins having a tonic-clonic seizure in bed?

options.A: Position the patient on their side and protect the head from injury
options.B: Force a padded wooden tongue depressor between the teeth firmly
options.C: Restrain all four limbs tightly to stop the violent shaking movements
options.D: Leave the bedside immediately to find the attending senior physician

explanation: Side-lying prevents aspiration of secretions, and padding protects against trauma, whereas restraints and mouth objects cause harm. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h7)

question: What instruction should a nurse give a patient regarding missed anti-seizure medication doses?

options.A: Stop taking the medication entirely for one week if a dose is missed
options.B: Double the next scheduled dose to make up for lost time
options.C: Never skip doses and consult a provider on what to do if missed
options.D: Crush the pills and mix them with alcohol for faster absorption

explanation: Consistency is vital, and patients need professional guidance rather than self-adjusting potent neuroactive medications. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h8)

question: Why is lifestyle counseling regarding sleep and alcohol important for patients with epilepsy?

options.A: Alcohol permanently repairs damaged neuronal ion channels
options.B: Sleep deprivation and alcohol withdrawal are major seizure triggers
options.C: These factors interfere with the digestive absorption of food
options.D: They prevent the brain from utilizing dietary carbohydrates

explanation: Both lack of rest and sudden changes in alcohol consumption lower the seizure threshold and provoke acute attacks. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h8)
